object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a certain amount on a certain cycle for a certain product.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a Subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered by the company, identified by a product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a Product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; identified by a plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a PricePlan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets -- the feature bundle (seats, API access, SSO); identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, absent for open-ended subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription, monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, and requester.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date
It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier of a PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: RequestDate
object_types.definition: The date a plan change was requested/made.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used for at least three distinct concepts: the billing PricePlan, the product FeatureBundle, and a sales-negotiated deal. The sales 'deal' concept is not modeled here since it was explicitly deferred to another meeting -- confirm whether it needs separate modeling.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated

ambiguities.description: Business policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run-to-term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided. Manual goodwill credits exist outside the modeled system but the rule that should govern them is unresolved.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Paused is described as a separate boolean flag that overlaps confusingly with the four-value Status, causing bugs (e.g. active-status queries incorrectly including paused subscriptions). It's unclear whether this should be reconciled into a fifth status or remain a separate flag; the business rule for interaction between Status and PausedFlag is not fully specified.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: When a company's account closes and reopens under the same company, it is treated as a brand-new Account with a new account number, deliberately losing history linkage to the prior account. It's ambiguous whether any conceptual link between old and new accounts of the 'same company' should be modeled (Tom flags this as a product concern) even though Finance requires no reuse.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between PlanChange's recorded new PricePlan/effective date and the Subscription's denormalised 'current PricePlan' field can disagree; the transcript states change history should win in case of conflict, implying a business rule/equality constraint that the current plan must always match the most recent effective change. This consistency rule is not formally enforced in the model and may require a subset/equality or derivation constraint.

source_references.excerpt: Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: MRR was explicitly decided to be a derived value (plan price normalized to a month) and not stored; confirming no fact type/attribute was created for it, but flag to ensure downstream consumers (e.g. reporting layer) understand it must be computed, not persisted on Subscription.

source_references.excerpt: So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts

ambiguities.description: The one-active-subscription-per-account-per-product rule (Halloway constraint) needs to be modeled as a constraint on the ternary combination of Account, Product, and 'active' status, but the current fact types split Account and Product into separate binary relations from Subscription. This composite business rule (uniqueness conditioned on active status) cannot be fully expressed with only binary internal_uniqueness constraints -- flag for review on whether a ternary or conditional constraint modeling is needed to capture 'active' qualification.

source_references.excerpt: So it's one active subscription per account per product. ... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level. Yes.
